summary.text: 汽 is built from the water side form 氵 and the sound element 气. An older dictionary account gives “water dried up,” with “tears falling” as an alternative; modern use centers on vapor and includes compounds for gasoline.

formation.text: 汽 is phonosemantic: 氵 marks the water category and 气 supplies the sound. A secondary proposal treats 气 as “air,” so the parts suggest steam, but the evidence does not establish that as an original intention.

components.text: 氵 is the conventional side form of 水 and marks the water category. Older dictionary glosses for 汽 include “water dried up” and, alternatively, “tears falling.”
气 is identified as the sound element. Zhengzhang Shangfang’s Old Chinese reconstruction gives the same form for 气 and 汽, consistent with that analysis.

sound.text: The supplied local Mandarin readings are qì for both 气 and 汽. In Zhengzhang Shangfang’s Old Chinese system, both are reconstructed as *kʰɯds; this historical comparison is consistent with the sound-element analysis.
Zhengzhang Shangfang reconstructs *kʰɯds for both 气 and 汽, a within-system comparison consistent with the phonetic role.

history.text: A dictionary preserves an analysis attributed to Shuowen and reports a small-seal form. No earlier graphic sequence or evidence of corruption is established.
Modern 汽 specializes in uses such as water vapor and gasoline, while 汔 is said to carry the older senses. The timing and process behind this distribution are unresolved.

uncertainties.text: The water-plus-air interpretation is a secondary proposal; whether it was also intended when 汽 was formed is unresolved.
The vapor sense is reported through Jiyun, but its earliest attestation and any semantic connection to “water dried up” or “tears falling” are unresolved.
The sources do not date the shift in dominant use or explain when the older senses came to be written with 汔. The Shijing phrase is reported, but its original written form is unresolved.

senses.text: An older dictionary account glosses 汽 as “water dried up.” The evidence does not date this use, so it cannot be identified here as the earliest attested meaning.
“Tears falling” is recorded as an alternative older gloss; its chronology relative to the other senses is unresolved.
A dictionary reports “water vapor” through Jiyun, but the attestation is not dated here.

senses.gloss: vapor and gas in modern compounds
senses.text: Modern 汽 occurs in compounds for water vapor and gasoline; these compound meanings do not by themselves establish separate single-character senses.

limitations.text: No semantic path from drying or tears to water vapor, or date for the shift in dominant use, is established. The report that 汔 now carries the older senses does not date or explain that distribution.

overview.text: 汽 uses 氵 to mark the water category and 气 as a sound element. Older dictionary glosses include “water dried up”; modern use centers on vapor and includes compounds for gasoline.

components.text: 氵 is the water side form, marking the relevant meaning category.
气 is the sound-bearing element in the supported analysis.

relationships.text: In 汽, 氵 marks the water category and is the side form of 水.
The dictionary analysis identifies 气 as the sound element. Zhengzhang Shangfang Old Chinese reconstructs *kʰɯds for both 气 and 汽, consistent with that role.
